newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians see EMU endangered by Bundesbank row.
newsitem.headline: Italians see EMU endangered by Bundesbank row.

text.p: Italian newspapers said on Thursday the German government's defiance of Bundesbank objections to its plan to help Bonn qualify for EMU by revaluing gold reserves could backfire on Europe's grand single currency design.

"If it is unthinkable for a (monetary) union to be born without Germany, it is equally unthinkable for the union to be born in spite of the Bundesbank," Turin daily newspaper La Stampa said in a editorial.

The newspaper said Bonn's plan to revalue the central banks's gold reserves in order to give a much-needed injection of cash to public finances had played directly into the hands of the German central bank.

The Bundesbank was "happy to warn the world of German finance, of which it has blatantly assumed the leadership, that even if the single currency is born, it will be born weak, unreliable and subject to pollution from execrable politics."

La Stampa mused on the paradox of Germany's struggle to meet the Maastricht Treaty's strict qualifying criteria for membership of European economic and monetary union (emu) just as Italy appeared to be making good progress.
"As things stand we have a real paradox. Germany is outside the Maastricht criteria by more than other countries," it added.
One of the key targets set out in the treaty requires EMU aspirants to bring their public sector deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratios down to three percent by the end of 1997.
"Even in Italy the deficit will exceed only slightly the fateful three percent but it will be on a downward path compared to past years while in Germany deficit and debt are growing."
Milan financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore, the mouthpiece of the Italian business establishment, sounded an even gloomier note in a front page commentary.

The Bundesbank's objections "can influence the selection of the countries joining the single currency, the nature of the Euro, the political outcome of the government and perhaps even the realisation of monetary union itself."

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has staked his survival on rail-roading Italy into EMU at the planned launch of the single currency, known as the Euro, in 1999 and is engaged in a race against time to wrestle Italy's public finances into shape.

A delay in the launch of EMU or abandonment of the whole single currency enterprise is a scenario which fills Italian leaders with dread. They fear all momentum could be lost behind their efforts to reform a creaking state.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect of the gold revaluation scheme, appeared to be playing with fire by taking on the Bundesbank head on, Il Sole said.
"Waigel has violated the Bundesbank taboo and the totem pole has fallen on him," it said, adding that the consequences of the dispute in the short term were grave.
"If the government hits back at the Bundesbank, Germans could definitively turn their backs on the prospect of a Euro which is not credible and not as strong as the mark," the newspaper said.
If Bonn were to give way to the central bank it would cast doubt on Germany's ability to have its public finances in a fit state to allow the single currency to be launched on time.
In that event a delay in EMU would be hard to avoid, said Milan daily Corriere della Sera.

"Faced with the possibility that not even Germany could reach the three percent threshold in the ratio between the public deficit and gross domestic product, the choice could be that of a delay rather than a loosening of the criteria," the newspaper said in an editorial
